title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol -- HTTP/1.1

hero.subtitle: The workhorse of the Web — persistent connections, chunked transfer, and content negotiation

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 is the most widely deployed version of HTTP and the workhorse of the modern Web. It introduces persistent connections, chunked transfer encoding, and many other improvements over HTTP/1.0.

RFC 2616 has been obsoleted by RFCs 7230-7235, which reorganize and clarify the specification without changing the protocol. The core protocol remains HTTP/1.1.
sections.eli5: Imagine a customer who has to leave the shop and come back in through the front door after every single question. That was HTTP/1.0. HTTP/1.1 lets the customer stay at the counter and ask many questions in a row.

sections.title: Connections
sections.content:
The most significant improvement in HTTP/1.1 is persistent connections:

Feature
HTTP/1.0
HTTP/1.1
Connection Lifetime
One request per connection
Multiple requests per connection
Default Behavior
Close after response
Keep-alive (persistent)
Pipelining
Not supported
Supported (multiple requests without waiting)

HTTP pipelining allows sending multiple requests without waiting for responses. However, it suffered from head-of-line blocking: a slow response blocks all subsequent responses. This limitation motivated HTTP/2.
sections.eli5: Before, every file needed its own new phone call. Now the browser keeps one call open and asks for the page, the picture, and the stylesheet one after another.

sections.title: Request
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 requires the Host header in every request, enabling virtual hosting (multiple websites on a single IP address):

HTTP/1.1 Request
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Accept: text/html, application/xhtml+xml
Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate
Connection: keep-alive
sections.eli5: When one building holds hundreds of shops, the postman needs the shop name on the envelope. The Host line is that name.

sections.title: Response
sections.content:
Responses may use chunked transfer encoding, allowing the server to send data in pieces without knowing the total size in advance:

Chunked Transfer Encoding
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Content-Type: text/html

12
<html><body>Hello 
14
World!</body></html>
0

Each chunk starts with its size in hexadecimal followed by CRLF, then the data, then another CRLF. A chunk of size 0 signals the end of the message body.
sections.eli5: A shopkeeper can start handing over a long story in pieces without knowing how long it is, and says "that was the last piece" with an empty one.

sections.title: Methods
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 adds PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE to the GET, HEAD and POST of HTTP/1.0 (CONNECT is also reserved for proxy tunnelling):

GETRetrieve a resource
HEADRetrieve headers only
POSTSubmit data for processing
PUTReplace the target resource entirely
DELETERemove the target resource
OPTIONSDescribe communication options for the target
TRACELoop-back test along the path to the target
sections.eli5: Each method is a verb: fetch this, show me just the label, send you this, swap it, throw it away, or tell me what I may do.

sections.title: Caching
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 introduces a comprehensive caching model using the Cache-Control header:

no-cacheMust revalidate with origin server before use
no-storeDo not store any part of the request or response
max-age=NResponse is fresh for N seconds
publicResponse may be cached by any cache
privateResponse is intended for a single user only
sections.eli5: Cache-Control is a sticky note on the answer saying how long you may keep your copy before asking again, and whether you may keep it at all.

sections.title: Content Negotiation
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 allows clients and servers to negotiate the best representation of a resource using Accept headers:

Accept
Specifies preferred media types: Accept: text/html, application/json;q=0.9
Accept-Encoding
Specifies preferred content encodings: Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate
Accept-Language
Specifies preferred languages: Accept-Language: en-US, fr;q=0.5

The quality factor (q) ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 being most preferred. If omitted, it defaults to 1. The server selects the best available representation based on these preferences.
sections.eli5: The browser says "I would like it in English, and squashed if possible", and the server picks the best version it has.

references.text: Fielding, R. and J. Reschke, "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Message Syntax and Routing", RFC 7230, June 2014.
Berners-Lee, T., Fielding, R., and H. Frystyk, "Hypertext Transfer Protocol -- HTTP/1.0", RFC 1945, May 1996.

subtitle: The workhorse of the Web — persistent connections, chunked transfer, and content negotiation
summary: RFC 2616 is the 1999 revision of HTTP/1.1. It made connections persistent by default, required a Host header so one IP address can serve many sites, added chunked transfer coding, a Cache-Control caching model and content negotiation with Accept headers. RFCs 7230-7235 and later RFCs 9110-9112 replaced the document but kept the protocol.

eli5.summary: It is the rulebook for how a web browser and a website talk, now letting them keep chatting on one phone line instead of hanging up after every sentence.

questions: what is a persistent connection in http
why does http 1.1 require a host header

tldr.problem: HTTP/1.0 opened a new TCP connection for every request, could not tell which site was wanted on a shared IP address, and had thin caching rules.
tldr.mechanism: HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default, requires a Host header, adds chunked transfer coding, a Cache-Control model and Accept-header content negotiation.
tldr.outcome: It became the web's workhorse for over two decades; RFCs 7230-7235 and then 9110-9112 replaced the document but kept the protocol.

facts.label: Methods
facts.value: OPTIONS, GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, TRACE, CONNECT

facts.label: Connections
facts.value: Persistent by default; Connection: close opts out

today: The document is obsolete, but HTTP/1.1 is still everywhere. RFCs 7230-7235 (2014) split and clarified it, and RFCs 9110-9112 (2022) replaced those. Pipelining turned out to be fragile and is rarely used; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 instead multiplex requests over one connection. Persistent connections, the Host header, chunked coding and Cache-Control all survive in current HTTP.
